results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 78 outline summaries match the controlling idea of the aligned spec paragraph (p01-p78) in spec order; e.g. Concepts ¶1 'search document / index' = p09, Choosing an Engine ¶2 'licensing no longer differentiates' = p54, Failure Modes ¶2-5 = p68-p71.

results.draft_locus: Concepts: What a Listing Search Layer Is ¶1
results.quote: Ingrid's questions need precise terms. **Search document.** The denormalized representation of one listing in the index
results.finding: The outliner needed two summaries ('definition of search document / definition of index'). The spec pairs the two terms as one idea (the unit and the set that holds it), but the draft runs the section bridge, a bold-headed 'Search document.' entry and a separate bold 'index' definition into one unit, so it reads as two glossary entries; flow reader A (point f) also found the start of the glossary hard to see here.
Every other unit (77 of 78) received a single-idea summary.

Every unit ties to a supporting claim: scene and concepts to S1/S2/S4/S6, architecture to S2/S6, document to S3, topology and read path/reindexing/capacity to S5, write path to S4, engine and in-practice to S6, closing group to all six. The licensing paragraph (Choosing an Engine ¶2) supports S6 (engine judged by fit, not licence).

Each table is framed by a sentence stating what it shows (component table 'what each component owns and what it must not own'; topology 'most of the options in use'; caches 'each has its own invalidation story'; engines 'what is documented, with dates'; criteria followed by 'None of these is decisive alone'; trade-offs and verticals tables stated). Figures 1-6 carry explanatory captions. Quotations (Solr cache clearing -> 'At peak, warming never caught up'; nested 'typically expensive'; mapping limit; Rightmove ad break -> 'capacity planning belongs on the same calendar'; Vinted 'boring') are followed by what they show. Vinted's confounded figures are explicitly qualified. The 'Vespa benchmark' sentence qualifies evidence never presented; it is recorded under flow_is_followable.

Read every transition_in at its boundary (77 boundaries). Each opening sentence carries the declared relationship and known information, e.g. p06 time 'The case for change arrived on Sunday 17 January 2027', p07 'The same review listed a slower problem', p09 'Ingrid's questions need precise terms', p20 'Three boundary rules matter more than the components', p27 'The workable design is a promotion rule', p34 'The trade-off is direct', p38 'Whatever the engine, five mitigations recur', p56/p57 contrast 'cannot be credited... What the series does show', p63 'Removal gets a tighter target', p67 'Each of these choices can fail', p77 'Ingrid's three questions now have answers', p78 'still has to understand what people type'. Weakest, still acceptable: p03 'The argument rests on one principle' leaves the cause_effect link to the high-write store implicit; p50 and p60 open on new material with the link carried by the heading.

Both flow readers describe the declared order (prerequisite order: scene, vocabulary, architecture, then large-to-small design from document to capacity, engine last, then the decision and a grouped closing set) and say the roadmap announces it; neither marks any section's position unclear. Points not counted as material because neither reader reported difficulty: forward references to the September 2027 decision in the latency budget and rebuild drill (A i, B d: 'Both are fine as forward references' / 'I did not get lost'); 'read model' in the opening (B j; on audience.already_knows); optional moves of Trade-offs or Vertical Differences (preferences).

results.finding: The introduction opens with a bridge from Part III's publication pipeline and a direct claim (listing search behaves like a high-write operational store), states the principle and a roadmap; it is none of placeholder, restated question, dictionary, 'dawn of man' or book report.

'From Engine to Intent' answers Ingrid's three questions with specifics drawn from the body, introduces no new subtopic, holds no new evidence, does not open with 'in conclusion' and ends on a problem_solution hand-off to query understanding rather than a rephrased thesis.

The conclusion states what no single section does: the answers to the three questions name no engine (must-be-true: listing-owned version, sourced documents, removal lane and objective, quarterly drill; shared: engine operations, indexer, contract, capacity; different: schemas, analyzers, ranking), and why it matters: the brown-out came from how the index was run, and the 2029 review becomes an adapter change rather than a rewrite.
Returns to the scene's Sunday-evening brown-out ('came from how the index was run at the peak, not from which engine ran it') and to Ingrid's three questions, as callback.to names.

The intro-only reader predicted, in order: Veldmark's three engines and the Sunday brown-out, the terms, the index as rebuildable read model, document, topology, write path, read path with facets and caching, reindexing, capacity, engine choice last, the September 2027 decision, trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, Chief Architect's view and review questions; evidence: public engineering accounts with Vinted above all, engine documentation and fictional Veldmark; tone declarative and practitioner-facing. Matches the roadmap and AC-2's expected answer (Tradeyard is not named but the brown-out is).

results.draft_locus: From Engine to Intent ¶1
results.quote: What must be true of any index: every document comes from the event stream and the system of record under a listing-owned version, removals take their own lane and objective, and a quarterly drill proves the rebuild.
results.finding: The cold reader names the three individually harmless causes (campaign ~30% above peak, a reindex committing into the live collection, commits clearing the filter and query-result caches browse traffic needed), the alias reindex with versioned backfill away from the peak planned with marketing, and decides the search contract and an index rebuildable from the event stream before any engine change, with engine choice then a workload decision via shadow traffic. It does not name the regular rebuild drill or removal latency as its own objective among the pre-engine decisions, two of the four the expected answer lists. The draft states them (conclusion, Chief Architect's decisions) but never gives the spec's takeaway as a course of action tied to engine change ('... prove the rebuild every quarter and give removal its own lane before deciding any engine change'); the decision's three conditions (p61) list only the contract, sourced documents and Vespa deferral, so a reader does not attach the drill and removal lane to 'before the engine'.

The cold reader uses the promotion rule (typed fields only for keys the category schema flags as filter, facet or sort; the rest in one flattened field, exact-value only), names the attribute dictionary as decider with promotion a reviewed schema change ('No engineer maps a field that the schema does not flag'), cites the 1,000-field default mapping limit with memory, merge and cluster-state costs, nested objects as hidden Lucene documents (30 attributes -> 31 documents), and normalized dictionary values upstream. Matches the expected answer.

The cold reader names the unversioned late 'price changed' applied after 'sold' (Ghost Inventory, hard to test as a race), a per-listing monotonic sequence owned by the aggregate as external version for every write including deletes (not Kafka offsets, which break on repartitioning), removals on a priority lane ahead of fan-out, bulk feeds in their own rate-limited lane, removal latency measured per operation and reason as a named objective (10 s p95 at Veldmark), and a read-path status recheck. Matches the expected answer.
